body: Every evening at the corner by the chemist, a woman walking home from the bus with a carrier bag in each hand crosses the road. Ten past six on a Friday, and she does it again. There is no reason to cross there. The pavement is better on the side she has left. She has been doing it for two years and it adds about eleven minutes to a walk that ought to take twenty. On the far pavement she passes a launderette and a shop that sells phone cases. At her door she puts both bags down to find her keys and notices that her hands are not quite steady, and she goes in and puts the kettle on.

That detour is an achievement and nobody in her life knows it is happening. It is also, precisely, a system being held in place — eleven minutes a day, five days a week, indefinitely, against something that has not moved an inch since the day she started walking the long way.

The first achievement is stopping, and it is enormous. It is also, on its own, a holding action: a state maintained by effort, day after day, against a pull that has gone nowhere. People sustain that for years. It is entirely genuine and it is exhausting in a way that is very hard to describe to anybody who has not done it.

It is worth taking the word sober literally, because it is a word about absence. Sobriety is defined by what is not happening. That makes it measurable, which is useful — you can count the days. But it also means the achievement can only ever be maintained rather than completed, because an absence has to be produced again every evening. Strength is the other kind of word. It describes a capacity rather than a gap: what a person can carry, what they can be near without effort, what they can do with an empty Friday. One of these can be held by will. The other has to be built, out of material, over a long time.

There is a frequency set aside for this on the band. HM 391.50 — Strong Sober — is assigned and in build, not yet on air, still silent. The dial itself runs from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70 and carries 121 stations, of which 46 are playing at this moment.

The second job is the expensive one and it comes with nothing attached. Sobriety is a state you can hold by force. Strength is what means you no longer have to — and there is no chip for it, no anniversary, no round of applause in a church hall. It is built out of unglamorous material: somewhere to be, someone who will pick up the phone, something to do with the hands, a reason to be up and dressed at eight on a Saturday morning. None of that is about the substance at all, which is exactly why it works.

The culture around this is not much help, in either direction. The stories almost all end at the moment of stopping — the bottle poured down the sink, the last scene in the car park. That is where the film finishes and where the actual work begins, and a person who has been handed that shape expects the hard part to be behind them at precisely the moment it is not. Then the other half of the culture treats a person as permanently eight hours from the edge, in a language that leaves no room for anybody ever having been rebuilt.

Conflating the two does damage in both directions and it is worth being specific about how. Somebody white-knuckling it for a decade gets told they are fine because they have not relapsed, and the fact that it is still costing them everything they have goes unnoticed by everyone including them. And somebody who genuinely has been remade — whose evenings are full, whose phone rings, who has not thought about it in months — is told to stay on guard forever, in terms that quietly inform them that the best version of their life is a permanent siege.
There is a serious model behind that second message, and it deserves better than a caricature.

The vigilance model says the thing is never gone and the day you believe you are safe is the day you are in danger. It has an enormous amount of evidence behind it and it has kept a very large number of people alive. It is honest about relapse in a way that motivational material never is. But look at what it does to a life over a long time. It makes the substance the permanent organising centre — the thing every evening is measured against, the subject of every anniversary, the first fact about the person in every room they walk into. A life arranged entirely around not drinking is still a life arranged around drink.
The absence has to be filled with something, or it stays an absence.

It is twenty to eight on a Saturday morning and a man of about fifty is unlocking a scout hut with a key that sticks, because the boiler needs twenty minutes. He puts the urn on. He sets out the circle, twelve chairs, always twelve even when there are seven, and he opens a window because the room smells of feet. A younger man arrives early and helps with the chairs and asks him, not quite casually, how long he has got. He has to stop and work it out. He gets it wrong, corrects himself, and goes back to the urn — and the reason he had to count is that he had stopped counting somewhere around the fourth year, when the mornings filled up and the number stopped being the most interesting thing about the week.

He is not more sober than the woman crossing the road. He is doing something different: the evenings and the mornings have been rebuilt underneath him, and the thing he is not doing has stopped being the load-bearing fact of the day.

The vigilance people are right about one thing and it should not be smoothed over. Strength does not confer immunity. People who had genuinely rebuilt — a job, a marriage, a room they were needed in — have gone back, after a bereavement or a diagnosis or nothing anybody could name afterwards. And there is no instrument that tells a person from the inside which of the two they currently have. The man with the urn cannot prove he is not the woman with the eleven-minute detour. Nobody gets a certificate.

But that uncertainty is not a defect in the arrangement. It is what strength is. It was never a possession to be issued and then owned; it is a direction, and it is maintained the same way a house is maintained, by somebody doing small unremarkable things to it continually. Anybody selling a permanent cure is lying, and anybody selling permanent siege is selling despair, and the truth sits in the unglamorous middle where most true things live: you build, and you keep building, and the building is what makes the not-drinking eventually stop being the point.

So the two achievements are not stages of one thing, and they are certainly not the same thing wearing different clothes. Stopping is the entry requirement — the door, not the room. What happens after it is the actual subject: a Friday evening that has somewhere to go, a Saturday morning that somebody is waiting for you at, an hour between six and eight that is filled rather than survived. That is slower work than stopping and much less dramatic, and it is the part almost nobody is congratulated for.
All of which is theory until it is Friday at six o’clock. So here is the part that is not theory.

The dial carries four kinds of programming and it is worth knowing they are there. Most of the band is music — praise and worship, contemporary, gospel, hymns, country. There is teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened and explained rather than sung. There is family programming, which is simply safe: entertaining, clean, and playable in a room with children in it whether or not every track names God out loud. And there are the international stations, hosted in their own languages for the nations rather than translated into them afterwards. Four kinds, one dial, and no menu to work through to reach them.

If you want somewhere to start, start at HM 315.20 — Corner Cipher. It is the Christian rap frequency on this band, and it is the right one for this argument. Most of that music is made by people who did not come out of anything cleanly, and it says so, in plain words, without the soft focus religious material about recovery usually applies. It is not soothing and it is not meant to be. An empty evening does not need calm; it needs company, and specifically the company of somebody who is not pretending. Put it on in a flat where the quiet has got loud and the room fills up with voices who have been where you are and are talking about something else now, which is the whole trick.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone is nearest, press play, and it plays — it is deliberately built for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It is free, it keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band learns which frequencies people are really reaching for, which is how the next station gets built.

So take this as an invitation rather than an offer. The evening still has to go somewhere, and it will go somewhere whether or not anybody plans it. Put HM 315.20 on at six on Friday, before the quiet arrives rather than after, and let it run while you do the washing up and answer a message and find something to do with your hands. It is one of the ordinary materials the second job is built out of, and the second job is the one that finishes.
